# RepoSentinel rule reference

<!-- Generated by scripts/generate_rules_doc.py from the rule definitions in
     src/reposentinel/checks/. Edit those, then re-run the script. -->

Every finding is a **potential indicator** that a person should review. No
rule confirms that a vulnerability is exploitable or that a credential is
valid, and no rule contacts any external service.

* **Severity** describes the likely impact *if* the finding is a true
  positive: `high` (direct compromise of credentials, code or CI is plausible),
  `medium` (a meaningful weakness or exposure that usually needs another
  factor), `low` (hardening opportunity), `info` (worth knowing, probably fine).
* **Confidence** describes how likely the match is a true positive, based on
  how distinctive the pattern is.
* Rule IDs are stable. Findings imported from an optional integration use the
  tool's own rule name with a prefix, for example `gitleaks:github-pat`.
* The **rule version** increases whenever a rule's matching changes.
  `reposentinel compare` reports findings of a rule whose version differs
  between the two scans as "Not comparable".
* **When a re-check no longer detects it** says what "Not detected on
  re-check" can *not* show for that rule. No re-check shows that a problem
  is fixed.

## RS-GHA-001

**Untrusted input expanded inside a script**: check `github-actions`, default severity `high`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A run: step, or an actions/github-script script, contains a ${{ }} expression that attacker-controlled data can reach, such as an issue title, pull request body, comment or branch name. GitHub pastes the value into the script before it runs, so crafted input can execute arbitrary commands on the runner.

**Why this severity.** High: successful injection runs attacker code with the job's GITHUB_TOKEN and any secrets available to it. Confidence is medium because exploitability depends on the trigger (who can open issues or pull requests) and on the job's permissions, which this rule does not evaluate.

**How to fix.** Pass the value through an environment variable and use it as a quoted shell variable, e.g. env: TITLE: ${{ github.event.issue.title }} and then run: echo "$TITLE". Never place expressions containing user-controlled data directly inside a script.

**Limitations and false positives.** Recognises a fixed list of well-known attacker-controllable contexts. Values that become untrusted indirectly (step outputs, env values, toJSON(github.event), bracket syntax such as github.event['issue']) are not detected. Composite actions are not analysed. Expressions that can only produce true or false (a single contains, startsWith or endsWith call, a comparison, or a negation, without && or ||) are not reported. The rule does not check whether the trigger actually provides the context, so a context that is always empty for that trigger is still reported.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** Moving the value into env: is the right fix, but then using it unsafely in the script (for example eval "$TITLE") is not detected, and contexts that become untrusted indirectly are not followed.

**References:** <https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-untrusted-input/>

## RS-GHA-002

**pull_request_target workflow checks out pull request code**: check `github-actions`, default severity `high`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** The workflow runs on pull_request_target, which executes with the base repository's secrets and a write-capable token, and it explicitly checks out the pull request's code. If a later step builds, installs or runs that code, a pull request from a fork can steal secrets or push to the repository (a 'pwn request').

**Why this severity.** High: this pattern has led to real repository compromises. Confidence is medium because a workflow that only reads the checked-out files, without executing them, may be safe.

**How to fix.** Use the pull_request trigger to build and test untrusted code. If pull_request_target is needed (for example to label or comment), do not check out the pull request head, or split the work into an unprivileged pull_request workflow and a privileged workflow that only consumes its artifacts. Set persist-credentials: false and minimal permissions.

**Limitations and false positives.** Detects actions/checkout steps whose ref or repository refers to the pull request's code (github.event.pull_request.head.*, github.event.pull_request.merge_commit_sha, github.head_ref, refs/pull/...). Other ways to fetch pull request code (git commands in run steps, other actions, workflow_run triggers) are not detected.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** Fetching the pull request with git commands in a run: step, or with another action, is not detected.

**References:** <https://securitylab.github.com/resources/github-actions-preventing-pwn-requests/>

## RS-GHA-003

**Third-party action not pinned to a commit SHA**: check `github-actions`, default severity `medium`, confidence `high`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A step or reusable workflow uses a third-party action by tag or branch (e.g. owner/action@v3) instead of a full 40-character commit SHA. Tags and branches can be moved by the maintainer, or by anyone who compromises their account, to point at malicious code.

**Why this severity.** Medium: exploitation requires compromising the upstream action, but when that happens every workflow using a movable reference runs the attacker's code with its own secrets, as happened in the 2025 tj-actions/changed-files incident.

**How to fix.** Pin to the full commit SHA of a reviewed release and record the version in a comment, e.g. uses: owner/action@<40-character-sha> # v3.1.0. Dependabot can keep SHA pins up to date.

**Limitations and false positives.** Actions owned by the 'actions' and 'github' organisations are not reported, to reduce noise; pinning them is still good practice. Docker references (docker://) and local actions (./path) are not evaluated. A SHA pin does not make the pinned code trustworthy.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** A SHA pin is not checked for trustworthiness: pinning to a malicious or compromised commit satisfies the rule.

## RS-GHA-004

**Workflow grants write-all permissions**: check `github-actions`, default severity `medium`, confidence `high`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** permissions: write-all gives the GITHUB_TOKEN write access to every scope (contents, packages, pull requests and more).

**Why this severity.** Medium: not exploitable on its own, but it turns any other weakness in the workflow (such as RS-GHA-001) into full write access to the repository.

**How to fix.** Replace write-all with the minimum scopes needed, e.g. permissions: contents: read, and grant write scopes only to the specific jobs that need them.

**Limitations and false positives.** Only the literal value write-all is reported. Broad explicit grants and missing permissions blocks (which fall back to the repository's default token permissions) are not evaluated.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** Only the literal value write-all is reported. Broad explicit write scopes are not, so replacing write-all with many write scopes is not detected.

## RS-HYG-001

**Environment (.env) file present**: check `hygiene`, default severity `medium`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A dotenv-style file (.env, .env.local, production.env, ...) exists in the repository tree. These files conventionally hold API keys, passwords and connection strings for local use, and are often committed by mistake.

**Why this severity.** Medium when the root .gitignore does not appear to ignore the file, because it is then easy to commit (or already committed). Reported as info when a root .gitignore pattern matches, because the file is then probably a local, untracked copy.

**How to fix.** Make sure the file is not tracked ('git ls-files <path>' prints nothing) and is listed in .gitignore. Commit a .env.example with placeholder values instead. If the file was ever committed, rotate every secret in it: it remains in Git history.

**Limitations and false positives.** RepoSentinel does not run Git, so it cannot tell whether the file is tracked. Only the root .gitignore is consulted, with simplified matching (nested .gitignore files, global excludes and .git/info/exclude are not read). Template files such as .env.example, .env.sample and .env.template are not reported.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** The rule checks file names only. A renamed file (for example settings.cfg) can still hold the same secrets, and a file deleted now is still in Git history.

## RS-HYG-002

**Private key or keystore file**: check `hygiene`, default severity `medium`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A file with a name conventionally used for private keys or keystores was found: SSH private keys (id_rsa, id_ed25519, ...), PKCS#12 bundles (.p12, .pfx), Java keystores (.jks, .keystore) or PuTTY private keys (.ppk).

**Why this severity.** Medium: the name strongly suggests key material, but the file may be a test fixture. When the content is a recognisable PEM private key, RS-SEC-001 also reports it at high severity.

**How to fix.** Remove the file from the repository and from Git history, replace the key or certificate if it was real, and keep key material in a secret manager or outside the repository.

**Limitations and false positives.** Name-based only. Keys stored under other names, including *.pem and *.key (which are also used for certificates and unrelated formats), are not reported by this rule; PEM private keys are covered by RS-SEC-001 whatever their name. Android debug keystores are a common, usually harmless, match.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** The rule checks file names only. Key material under another name is not detected, and a removed key file stays in Git history and stays valid until the key is replaced.

## RS-HYG-003

**Plain-text credential store file**: check `hygiene`, default severity `high`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A file whose purpose is to store credentials in plain text was found: .git-credentials (Git's credential store), .netrc or _netrc (logins for curl, FTP and Git) or .pgpass (PostgreSQL passwords).

**Why this severity.** High: these files exist to hold reusable passwords or tokens in clear text. Confidence is medium because the file could be a deliberately fake fixture.

**How to fix.** Remove the file from the repository and from Git history, change every password or token it contained, and keep such files in your home directory, where these tools look for them by default.

**Limitations and false positives.** Name-based; empty files are ignored. Other credential files (cloud CLI configuration, .npmrc or .pypirc containing tokens, application configuration) are not covered.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** The rule checks file names only. Credentials kept under another name are not detected, and removed credentials stay in Git history and stay valid until they are changed.

## RS-SEC-001

**Private key block**: check `secrets`, default severity `high`, confidence `high`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A PEM, OpenSSH or PGP private key header was found. Whoever holds a private key can impersonate the server, user or signing identity it belongs to.

**Why this severity.** High: a real private key usually grants direct access or signing ability. It is not rated higher because the key may be a test key or already revoked, which RepoSentinel cannot determine.

**How to fix.** Remove the key from the repository and from Git history, then treat it as compromised: revoke or replace it and store the new key outside the repository (a secret manager, CI secret, or a local file listed in .gitignore).

**Limitations and false positives.** Detects the header line only and does not check that a valid key follows. Keys in other encodings (PKCS#12, Java keystores, base64 blobs) are not detected by this rule. Test fixtures in cryptography projects are a common false positive.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** A key that was re-encoded (for example base64) or moved to a file that was not examined is not detected. A removed key stays in Git history and stays usable until it is replaced.

## RS-SEC-002

**AWS access key ID**: check `secrets`, default severity `medium`, confidence `high`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A value in the format of an AWS access key ID was found (AKIA... for long-term keys, ASIA... for temporary ones).

**Why this severity.** Medium: the key ID alone does not grant access, but it identifies an AWS credential and is rarely committed without its secret access key nearby (see RS-SEC-003).

**How to fix.** Look for the matching secret access key. If the key is real, deactivate and delete it in AWS IAM, review CloudTrail for unexpected use, and obtain credentials at runtime instead (IAM roles, IAM Identity Center, or CI-provided secrets).

**Limitations and false positives.** Matches the documented key-ID format only and does not check that the key exists. Values containing 'EXAMPLE' (used throughout AWS documentation) and placeholders whose last 16 characters are one repeated character (AKIAXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX) are ignored.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** A key ID that was split, encoded or moved to a file that was not examined is not detected. A removed key stays valid until it is deactivated in AWS.

**References:** <https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html>

## RS-SEC-003

**AWS secret access key assignment**: check `secrets`, default severity `high`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A 40-character value assigned to a name such as aws_secret_access_key or SecretAccessKey was found.

**Why this severity.** High: together with its key ID, a secret access key grants whatever AWS permissions the key has. Confidence is medium because the rule relies on the variable name.

**How to fix.** Deactivate and delete the key pair in AWS IAM, review CloudTrail for unexpected use, and obtain credentials at runtime instead of storing them in files.

**Limitations and false positives.** Only detects values assigned to a recognisable name on the same line. Secrets stored under other names, split across lines, or encoded are missed. Values containing 'EXAMPLE' are ignored.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** Renaming the variable stops this name-based rule from matching. The key stays valid until it is deactivated in AWS, and stays in Git history.

## RS-SEC-004

**GitHub token**: check `secrets`, default severity `high`, confidence `high`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A value in a documented GitHub token format was found: personal access tokens (ghp_, github_pat_), OAuth tokens (gho_), user-to-server (ghu_), server-to-server (ghs_) or refresh tokens (ghr_).

**Why this severity.** High: a valid token acts as the user or app it was issued to, often with write access to repositories.

**How to fix.** Revoke the token in GitHub (Settings > Developer settings, or the organisation's token management page), review the account's security log, and supply tokens through CI secrets or a credential helper instead of source files.

**Limitations and false positives.** Matches token formats only; it does not validate the checksum or contact GitHub. Legacy 40-character hexadecimal tokens are not detected. Placeholders whose random part is one repeated character (ghp_xxxx...) are ignored.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** A token split into pieces or encoded is not detected. A removed token stays valid until it is revoked, and stays in Git history.

**References:** <https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/about-authentication-to-github#githubs-token-formats>

## RS-SEC-005

**Credentials embedded in a URL**: check `secrets`, default severity `medium`, confidence `medium`, rule version 1.

**What it detects.** A URL of the form scheme://user:password@host was found, for example a database connection string with an inline password.

**Why this severity.** Medium: such URLs often point at development databases, but they are copied into logs, error messages and shell history, and production values do end up committed.

**How to fix.** Move the password out of the URL into an environment variable or secret store and build the URL at runtime. Change the password if it was ever used for a real system.

**Limitations and false positives.** Obvious placeholders (such as 'password', 'changeme', '${DB_PASSWORD}', '<password>' or '****') are ignored, which also hides real passwords that happen to equal a placeholder. Passwords containing spaces, quotes or an unescaped '/', '?' or '#' are not matched. The evidence never shows the user name, password or host name (host names can reveal internal systems); open the file at the reported line to see which system it is.

**When a re-check no longer detects it.** A password written in another form, or moved to a file that was not examined, is not detected. Change the password if it was ever used for a real system.
